title: German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty
subtitle: How the occupiers revised the partition and sought to make it permanent
body:
On September 28, 1939, Warsaw accepted military defeat while Germany and the Soviet Union claimed the authority to decide what defeat meant for the whole country. In Moscow, Ribbentrop and Molotov put their names to a treaty that described Poland as a former state and reserved its reorganization to the two invaders. The city’s surrender furnished no Polish consent to that claim. Fighting continued elsewhere, and Polish diplomats were preparing to reject the settlement. The treaty’s central problem was already apparent: the occupiers could divide territory without compelling Poland or its allies to accept the political consequences. [1] [2] [3] The accompanying agreements show what consolidation required. The partners adjusted their territorial claims, provided for selected migrations, promised to suppress Polish agitation affecting one another’s areas, and prepared expanded economic exchange. Their joint declaration then urged Britain and France to end the war against Germany. Those commitments belonged to one diplomatic effort: secure the gains of invasion, limit friction between the occupiers, and persuade the outside world to treat the result as settled. [4] [5] [6] [7] The August pact had opened the possibility of partition; the German and Soviet invasions supplied the force. September’s settlement revised the bargain in light of what both governments now wanted. This study follows the treaty and its immediate implementation and reception through October. Later developments are dated explicitly, because signature, demarcation, movement of prisoners, and the creation of occupation administrations followed different schedules. Warsaw’s capitulation did not end organized resistance. Modlin surrendered on September 29; the Hel Peninsula held until October 2; the final major campaign battle, around Kock, ended with capitulation on October 6. These were decisions by commanders responsible for particular forces, under circumstances that differed from one position to another. Surrender, capture, and the exhaustion of a formation cannot by themselves establish desertion or mutiny. More immediately for the negotiators in Moscow, continuing resistance contradicted the appearance of a completed settlement. Germany and the Soviet Union were asserting political finality before the campaign itself had ended. [8] [9]

Returning to Moscow with a different bargain

The secret protocol of August 23 had left some matters open. It envisaged a division of interests in Polish territory approximately along the Narew, Vistula and San, but reserved the question of whether an independent Polish state should survive. That reservation was disappearing by late September. In a telegram describing his meeting with Stalin and Molotov on September 25, the German ambassador, Friedrich-Werner von der Schulenburg, reported Stalin’s opposition to leaving a Polish rump state. Stalin presented such a state as a potential cause of future disagreement between the two powers. This was a German diplomatic account of the conversation, but it recorded a specific proposal subsequently reflected in the settlement. [10] [11] Stalin offered Germany the Lublin province and the part of Warsaw province extending to the Bug, in exchange for relinquishing German claims to Lithuania. His intervention helps explain why the eventual boundary differed from the August arrangement. The revision was not simply the result of German troops having advanced farther than anticipated. Soviet leadership was actively bargaining over the shape of the occupation and the direction in which Soviet influence should expand. Berlin gained a larger share of central Poland; Moscow gained German acceptance of its predominant interest in Lithuania. The same conversation linked agreement over Poland to further Soviet action in the Baltic region. [11] Ribbentrop arrived on the evening of September 27. A timetable in the papers of German diplomat Andor Hencke records a first meeting that night, further discussions on September 28, dinner at the Kremlin, and an act of Swan Lake. Talks resumed at midnight and signing followed at five in the morning. The sequence places the signatures in the early hours of September 29, although the instruments bear September 28. That dated agreement remains the historical reference point. The overnight schedule matters chiefly because it captures the concentrated negotiations required to turn Stalin’s proposal into several interlocking commitments. [12]

What five public articles tried to settle

The public treaty was short enough to conceal its ambition behind administrative language. Article I identified the boundary of German and Soviet interests through an attached map, with further description to follow. Article II declared the line definitive and rejected intervention by other powers. Article III assigned administrative reorganization west of the line to Germany and east of it to the Soviet Union. Article IV presented the settlement as a basis for friendship between their peoples. Article V required ratification but made the agreement effective upon signature. The preamble’s reference to the “former Polish state” was the political premise supporting the whole construction. [2] The public articles asserted an authority the signatories had obtained by force and Poland had never conceded. Article III’s allocation of administrative responsibility left each occupier substantial discretion over institutions and inhabitants on its side. Article II sought to protect that discretion from outside intervention. The treaty therefore made a territorial division and a political demand at the same time. Recognition by other governments would have helped remove Poland’s future from further negotiation; Polish rejection and continuing Allied war prevented that desired conclusion. [2] [3] The revised division placed much of the central stretch of the boundary on the Bug, farther east than the earlier Vistula division. A report sent from Berlin by the American chargé, Alexander Kirk, on September 29 described the published route from the vicinity of Lithuania through the northern river system, along the Bug and eventually to the San. It was a report of the German news agency’s description, rather than a field survey. Its value lies in showing what was being announced to the outside world: the partners had replaced a provisional arrangement with a declared territorial settlement, including a new allocation of land in central Poland. [13] Implementation required further decisions after the line had been declared definitive. Steinhardt’s dispatch of October 5 reported a supplementary protocol signed the previous day and a mixed commission to arrange frontier details; a later report recorded ratification on October 19. These stages explain how a treaty effective on signature could still leave work for surveyors and administrators. Their actions would translate the diplomatic division into crossing arrangements and jurisdictions. The interval is important to the atlas because the treaty date alone cannot establish the position of every unit or the date on which every locality experienced the new boundary. [14] [15]

Reading the atlas

A partition line is not a battlefront

The September 28 map shows an approximate trace of the agreed partition. It should not be read as proof that all troops had reached their final positions that day. The later demarcation work also means that the treaty date and the physical marking of the frontier must be kept separate. A diplomatic map records what governments agreed to claim; an operational map must establish where forces actually were. [14]

Lithuania in the balance

The territorial revision had another side that remained secret. Lithuania was transferred into the Soviet sphere of influence, while Germany acquired the specified additional Polish territory. The supplementary protocol also preserved a prospective German claim to a strip in southwestern Lithuania and protected existing German–Lithuanian economic agreements. These details expose the transactional character of the bargain. Lithuania was neither a defeated participant in the Polish campaign nor a consenting party to this agreement. Its future was being discussed as something two larger neighbors could exchange for advantages elsewhere. [16] Allocation to a sphere did not immediately annex Lithuania or install Soviet administration there. It changed the diplomatic conditions under which Moscow could make further demands. The Soviet–Lithuanian mutual assistance treaty of October 10 offered Lithuania Wilno—Vilnius in Lithuanian—and its surrounding district while permitting Soviet bases and garrisons on Lithuanian territory. Reporting the next morning, Steinhardt noted that the numbers and locations of those forces were left for a further agreement. A territorial gain that Lithuania had long sought was attached to a military concession that narrowed its freedom of action. [17] This sequence also changed the position of the people in Wilno without consulting them. The city had been in Poland before the invasions; it was now being transferred through an agreement between the Soviet Union and Lithuania. Soviet occupation and incorporation of Lithuania itself came in 1940 and must not be read backward into the September allocation. In autumn 1939, influence, basing rights, and direct administration were still distinct forms of power, acquired through different instruments. [17] [18] The southwestern strip remained a source of private maneuvering. Ribbentrop’s instructions of October 4, transmitted early on October 5, recorded that Molotov had informed the Lithuanian foreign minister of the confidential arrangement. Berlin now had to explain its own claim. The instructions presented the proposed transfer as a practical correction to an awkward border, while reserving Germany’s right to decide when it should occur. Germany also wanted Soviet troops kept out of the strip. The episode shows how a settlement advertised as clear and final could still contain deferred claims, controlled disclosures and competing preferences over implementation. [19]

Polish politics and populations behind the new line

The secret agitation protocol addressed an obstacle that a territorial line could not remove: Polish opposition might operate across both occupation zones. Each signatory promised to suppress Polish agitation in its territory when that activity affected the other party’s territory, and to exchange information on suitable measures. The obligation made the suppression of opposition a matter of mutual concern. It did not define a common police organization, name particular victims, or order a specific massacre. Those acts require their own evidence; the protocol establishes the commitment under which political cooperation could develop. [4] The wording also exposed the weakness in the treaty’s public claim. If Poland had simply vanished as a political community, its activity would hardly have required a separate secret agreement. The signatories anticipated that loyalties and opposition would survive across their new line. By describing such activity as agitation, they classified an obstacle to their settlement in the language of repression. That was their category, not a neutral judgment on the legitimacy of Polish resistance. [4] A confidential population protocol approached the inhabitants from a different direction. Moscow agreed not to obstruct the departure of German nationals and people of German descent who wished to move to Germany or German-administered territory. Transfers were to be conducted by German agents working with the local authorities, with emigrants’ property rights protected. Berlin assumed a corresponding obligation for people of Ukrainian or Belarusian descent in its area. The document’s language concerned people wishing to migrate. It was not a blanket authorization for every forced displacement that followed. Yet its categories showed the occupiers organizing movement according to ancestry across a frontier the affected population had not chosen. [5] The property guarantees in the migration protocol applied to specified emigrants, not to every household uprooted by conquest. Nor did the document give Polish and Jewish communities a corresponding collective choice about which state would rule them. Its categories created privileges for particular movements while the broader population remained subject to each occupier’s controls. The distinction between an agreement allowing selected people to leave and a system that compelled others to move is essential to the history of the following months. [5] Prisoners faced a separate sorting process. The Soviet Politburo’s resolution of October 2 directed the release of specified private soldiers from the Soviet-occupied eastern territories, retained others for road construction, and concentrated private soldiers from German-occupied districts pending negotiations with Germany. Officers and senior officials were assigned to special confinement; policemen and related categories were to be held at Ostashkov. Beria’s implementing orders on October 3 sought to prevent their release with ordinary soldiers. The IPN’s reconstruction records subsequent transfers to German custody during October and November. These were prisoner-management decisions, not the voluntary migration promised in the September protocol. A man’s home district and status could determine which power detained him, or whether he was retained for forced labor. [20]

The resources and railways inside the bargain

The economic correspondence accompanying the treaty is easily overshadowed by its map. It deserves attention because the new relationship had to function during a continuing European war. In an exchange of letters dated September 28, the Soviet government committed itself to developing a program of raw-material deliveries, to be compensated by German manufactured goods over a longer period. The parties proposed restoring trade to the highest volume previously reached and beginning negotiations promptly. This was a framework for expanded exchange, rather than a complete list of deliveries already made. [6] The letter’s delivery schedules created continuing obligations rather than a single balanced shipment. German negotiators still had to specify what would move, when it would move, and what Germany would provide in return. Steinhardt reported at the end of October that economic negotiations were still continuing. Their unfinished state limits any claim about the treaty’s immediate material effect: the promise of trade supported cooperation, but a promise was not proof of deliveries already made. [6] [15] The confidential letter made this economic geography unusually concrete. It promised facilitation of German transit toward Romania on the Upper Silesia–Lemberg–Kolomea railway and toward Iran, Afghanistan and the Far East. Its petroleum provision used the annual production of Drohobycz–Borysław to define an additional quantity, but specified that half would come from that district and half from other Soviet fields, in exchange for coal and steel piping. This detail qualifies the familiar association of partition with possession of resources: the arrangement combined a regional production benchmark with a wider Soviet supply obligation. It recorded a promise whose fulfillment still required deliveries. [21]

Poland refuses to disappear

The clearest Polish answer arrived in the language of diplomacy rather than a battlefield communiqué. On September 30, Ambassador Jerzy Potocki informed the United States, on his government’s instructions, that the Moscow agreement violated existing treaties and international law. Poland refused to recognize it and intended to recover its occupied territory and its people’s freedom and self-determination. The note was short, direct and addressed to another government. Its significance lay partly in the ordinary diplomatic act itself: the representative of the allegedly extinguished state was continuing to speak and be received as its representative. [3] Reconstituting authority required more than issuing a protest. Poland’s president and leading ministers were interned in Romania, with their freedom of movement and communication restricted. The Polish foreign ministry’s historical account identifies Ambassador Roger Raczyński as a crucial intermediary between the interned leadership and the politicians assembling in France. He helped secure the transfer of the presidency from Ignacy Mościcki to Władysław Raczkiewicz. This was practical institutional work under constraint: someone had to maintain contact, obtain decisions, and provide a basis on which diplomats and soldiers abroad could continue to act for Poland. [22] On September 30, Raczkiewicz became president and General Władysław Sikorski prime minister in France. The government moved to Britain only after France’s defeat in 1940; calling it the London government at this stage obscures where continuity was first rebuilt. Its survival mattered beyond formal recognition. Diplomatic missions could represent refugees and sustain the effort to assemble Polish forces abroad. The foreign ministry describes consular work issuing identity documents and providing limited aid in Romania. Such assistance could not undo occupation, but it gave displaced people a surviving Polish institution to approach. [23] [22] The United States gave an explicit answer of its own. A statement issued by Secretary of State Cordell Hull on October 2 affirmed that Washington continued to regard the Polish government as existing despite Poland’s subjection to force. The statement is recorded in an editorial note in the State Department’s documentary collection. Recognition was not military rescue, and the United States remained outside the European war. Nevertheless, this position contradicted the legal and political premise on which Berlin and Moscow had presented their settlement. The continued war against Germany and the survival of Polish diplomacy meant that the partition remained internationally disputed. [24]

London and Paris read the same treaty differently

The joint declaration issued with the treaty tried to turn the occupation of Poland into an argument for ending the European war. Germany and the Soviet Union announced that their settlement had created the basis for peace in eastern Europe, called for an end to the conflict between Germany and the Western powers, and assigned Britain and France responsibility if efforts to end it failed. They also promised consultation about further measures. The sequence of the argument was convenient for both signatories: their conquests were treated as settled before the opponents of those conquests were invited to make peace. [7] On October 3, Neville Chamberlain described the agreement in the House of Commons as an attempted fourth partition of Poland. He identified the frontier settlement, the peace declaration and the projected economic relationship as connected developments. Britain, he argued, had entered the war against a recurring pattern of German aggression; Poland’s defeat had not removed that reason. His response rejected the suggestion that successful conquest entitled Germany to dictate when the international consequences of its attack should end. The speech also made clear that further promises from Hitler’s government would be judged against its record of broken undertakings. [25] The parliamentary discussion was less uniform than that central statement suggests. In the same debate, David Lloyd George urged a different treatment of the Soviet role, while Labor’s David Grenfell condemned the Soviet intervention and argued that the presence of two aggressors did not diminish the wrong done to Poland. The exchange illustrates a continuing difficulty for British politics: opposition to Germany did not produce a single view of Moscow. Arguments about Soviet security, former imperial frontiers and future strategic rivalry could coexist with recognition that the Soviet Union had participated in Poland’s destruction. [25] Private British assessments were cautious about predicting an unlimited alliance. Joseph Kennedy’s report of September 30 described Foreign Office officials as expecting Moscow to benefit from a prolonged conflict among the Western powers while remaining outside that war. They considered direct Soviet military commitment to Germany unlikely, though the warmth of Ribbentrop’s reception caused concern. The British ambassador in Moscow even raised the possible value of trade incentives in influencing Soviet conduct. These were judgments about interests and possible policy, not privileged knowledge of Stalin’s future decisions. They help explain how condemnation of the partition could coexist with efforts to avoid extending the war to the Soviet Union. [26] French anxiety produced a warning whose certainty exceeded the evidence Bullitt could establish. On September 30, Alexis Léger, the foreign ministry’s secretary general, told him that Moscow had promised Germany 2,000 bombers for an attack on France. Bullitt argued that this would run against Soviet interests; Léger insisted and said the report was encouraging some parliamentarians to consider the peace proposal. The dispatch records a disputed intelligence claim and its reported political effect, not a confirmed Soviet commitment. Fear of a wider coalition could influence decisions before anyone had demonstrated that the coalition existed in the form described. [27] French concern did not immediately produce a decision to break with Moscow. On October 7, the French chargé there told Steinhardt that the developing partnership had caused him to reconsider his earlier opposition to a rupture. He was contemplating recommending a firmer policy, potentially including a break in relations, and asked how American representation of French interests might be arranged. He expressly described the inquiry as anticipatory. Preserving that qualification matters: a diplomat exploring a contingency was not announcing a decision by his government. [28] Publicly, Édouard Daladier insisted on security that would last. Chamberlain’s statement of October 12, replying to Hitler’s subsequent peace proposals, cited the French premier’s broadcast two days earlier and stressed the need for dependable guarantees. Britain and France would not accept conquest as a sufficient foundation for peace merely because Germany now offered negotiations. Their position sustained the war against Germany, although it had not saved Poland from occupation. For Poles, that distinction was painfully concrete: continued allied belligerency preserved a future possibility of liberation while leaving the immediate balance of force inside their country unchanged. [29]

Selling the peace in Germany and the Soviet Union

Reports collected by SOPADE, the German Social Democrats in exile, suggest why a peace appeal could have domestic force. They described hopes that the Polish campaign would be followed by a quick end to war and recorded resentment of blackout restrictions. In one southwest German report, residents in an unidentified town refused to enter shelters during an air-raid alarm on September 24, prompting police intervention. This was reported civilian noncompliance, not a military mutiny. The clandestine network was incomplete and inclined to notice discontent; its reports cannot measure national opinion. They nevertheless preserve evidence of reluctance and irritation beneath official declarations of unity. [30] Moscow’s public language moved decisively in support of the relationship. In his speech to the Supreme Soviet on October 31, Molotov defended German–Soviet friendship and presented Germany as seeking peace while Britain and France pursued the war for imperial aims. Steinhardt’s report noted Molotov’s argument that a strong Germany was necessary for European peace, together with his favorable account of the ongoing economic negotiations. This was an official justification of policy, not evidence that ordinary Soviet citizens had reached the same conclusions. It showed the Soviet leadership lending its authority to the diplomatic argument Germany wanted the Western powers to accept. [31]

The boundary as people encountered it

For refugees, the new boundary could convert a flight of uncertain duration into separation from home and relatives. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum records crossings becoming closed and guarded, and both Soviet and German border guards subjecting people without papers to arrest and arbitrary violence. Some refugees attempted clandestine passage. Others, exhausted and penniless, returned toward homes in German-occupied Poland. Their choices responded to the danger, resources, and information available at that moment. Returning did not mean they had judged Nazi rule safe; remaining displaced could itself appear impossible. [32] The contrast with the treaty’s provisions was severe. Commercial traffic was to receive negotiated transit arrangements, and selected ethnic groups were promised organized migration. An inhabitant trying to cross to rejoin a family had no comparable general entitlement under those agreements. The powers could facilitate movement when it served their arrangements while restricting it for people whose lives had crossed the new boundary long before the boundary existed. What appeared orderly in an exchange of diplomatic letters could make an ordinary journey dangerous. [5] [21] Przemyśl reveals what a transfer of control could conceal. Yad Vashem’s account dates German occupation to September 15 and records the murder of several hundred Jews and the burning of synagogues in the following days, before the city’s main part passed to Soviet rule. This was an attack on an established community whose schools, hospital, welfare institutions, political organizations, and places of worship had sustained local life. During the ensuing Soviet occupation, Jewish political parties were dissolved and communal institutions subordinated to municipal authority. The source does not date each of those changes to the transfer itself. Synagogues that remained open also provided relief to local people and refugees. Community assistance survived alongside attacks on communal autonomy; neither fact can erase the preceding murders or stand as a verdict on everyone’s response to Soviet power. [33] The treaty distributed control without creating the complete administrative machinery through which either occupier would govern. Germany’s annexation measures and the General Government belonged to the following month; the Soviet incorporation measures followed on **November 1–2**. Keeping those steps separate explains what the September agreement achieved: it reduced conflict between the invaders over their respective territorial claims, leaving each substantial room to impose its own institutions. The [study of October 26](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) examines the resulting German arrangements and the parallel Soviet process. [34] [35]

A settlement Poland refused

The treaty gave cooperation a wider institutional basis than the August pact. The signatories now assigned administration, defined categories of permitted movement, negotiated supply routes, and undertook to suppress cross-border opposition. The October treatment of prisoners shows another way in which the partition could organize people’s fates. These arrangements made occupation more manageable for its authors while leaving inhabitants subject to authorities they had not chosen. Their practical operation did not depend on Poland accepting the occupiers’ claim that its state had disappeared. [2] [4] [5] Yet the peace the signatories advertised failed to follow. Britain and France continued the war against Germany, and Poland’s government operated in France with continuing international recognition. Inside the occupied territory, the balance of force remained overwhelmingly with the invaders. Their next task was to turn control into sustained administration: offices, police powers, labor obligations, and rules governing property and residence. The October study examines that process. The September settlement had reduced conflict between the occupiers; it had not ended the conflict over Poland’s future. [29] [24]
author: R.G. Cruise
location: Moscow, occupied Poland and the European capitals
summary: The September treaty joined a revised territorial division to agreements on political suppression, selected migration, trade, and transit. Its implementation reached prisoners and refugees while Polish diplomacy and continued Allied war challenged the claim that Poland’s future was settled.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations identify the passages used and link back to their first appearance. Published treaty texts, German and American diplomatic records, parliamentary proceedings, and museum research were inspected, including retained full-text source copies. Original manuscripts were not consulted. Reports and official speeches preserve attributed claims; Léger’s bomber allegation remains unconfirmed. Daladier’s broadcast is cited through the British parliamentary record. The IPN prisoner account is a historical reconstruction in an investigation announcement, not a court finding; Yad Vashem’s Przemyśl entry was read in Hebrew. Signature, demarcation, ratification, population protocols, prisoner transfers, and later annexations are kept distinct.
